The Product Manager's Job and Mindset

What a product manager is actually responsible for, the language product teams use every day, and what changes when you build for African users. You finish the module able to frame a product problem as an outcome, a set of risks and a testable hypothesis.
What a product manager does: outcomes and the four product risks
Explain the difference between an output and an outcome, with an example
Name the four big product risks and who on a team usually owns each one
Spot the risk a feature idea has not yet addressed
Describe how a product manager works with design, engineering and the business

A product team can write excellent code and still fail. The app works, but people do not use it, or they use it and the business still loses money. The **product manager (PM)** is the person whose job is to reduce that danger. She does not usually write the code or draw the screens. She decides, with the team, **what problem to solve next, for whom, and how we will know it worked**.
A person presenting a product on a large screen
The PM explains why a product exists and what it must achieve, not only what it does.
Outputs versus outcomes

An **output** is something the team ships: a new screen, a feature, a release. An **outcome** is a change in what people do that matters to the business: more traders paying suppliers through the app, fewer failed deliveries, fewer customers calling support. Outputs are easy to count, so weak teams celebrate them. Strong teams measure outcomes, because a feature that nobody uses is cost without value.

A simple test: if you can tick it off as done on the day you release it, it is an output. If you must wait and watch user behaviour to know whether it happened, it is an outcome. A good PM can always say which outcome a piece of work is meant to move.
The four big risks

Marty Cagan of the Silicon Valley Product Group describes four risks that every product idea carries. Discovery work, which you will practise in Module 2, exists to reduce these risks **before** a team spends weeks building.
Risk
The question
Usually led by
Value
Will customers buy it, or will users choose to use it?
Product manager
Usability
Can users figure out how to use it?
Product designer
Feasibility
Can our engineers build it with the time, skills and technology we have?
Lead engineer
Business viability
Does it work for the rest of the business: legal, finance, sales, support, partners?

Notice that the PM owns two of the four. Value is about the customer: does this solve a problem painful enough that people change their behaviour? Viability is about the organisation: can we afford it, can support handle it, does it break a regulation or a partner agreement? A brilliant idea that fails either test is not ready.
The four risks every idea must pass
Value: will they use it?
Usability: can they use it?
Feasibility: can we build it?
Viability: does it work for us?
An idea is ready to build only when the team has evidence on all four, not just enthusiasm for one.
Worked example: testing a feature idea against the four risks
For example, Amaka is PM for a savings app used by market traders in Lagos. A director asks for a feature that lets traders lock savings for 90 days in exchange for a higher interest rate.
Value: Amaka asks what evidence exists that traders want to lock money away. She finds that 6 of the last 40 support chats asked about fixed savings. That is a signal, not proof.
Usability: the designer warns that many users read English as a second language, so the lock rules must fit in two short sentences with a clear penalty shown before confirming.
Feasibility: the lead engineer says the ledger can already hold balances with an end date, so a first version is about two weeks of work.
Viability: finance must confirm the business can pay the higher rate, and compliance must check what the licence allows. Amaka books both conversations before any build starts.
She writes the outcome she wants: more traders keeping savings in the app for at least 90 days, measured over the next quarter.

The idea moves forward only on value and feasibility. Amaka parks it until finance and compliance answer the viability questions, saving the team from building something that might have to be withdrawn.
Who the PM works with
**Engineers:** decide how to build, estimate effort, and warn about technical risk. Bring them into problems early, not just finished specifications.
**Designers:** shape the experience and test usability with real users.
**Business stakeholders** (sales, operations, finance, legal, support): bring constraints and customer signals. They are partners, not customers whose every request must be built.
**Users and customers:** the people whose behaviour decides whether the product succeeds.
A PM's week

In a typical week a PM might spend time talking to users or reading support messages, reviewing usage numbers, refining upcoming stories with engineers, checking designs with the designer, updating stakeholders on progress and decisions, and saying a respectful no to requests that do not serve the current outcome. The mix changes with the product's stage, but talking to users and making clear decisions should never disappear from the calendar.
Authority without command

Most PMs do not manage the engineers or designers they work with. Influence comes from clear reasoning, shared evidence and keeping promises. When you say no to a request, explain which outcome the alternative serves better.
The PM decides with the team what problem to solve, for whom, and how success will be measured.
Outputs are what you ship; outcomes are the changes in behaviour you want.
Every idea carries value, usability, feasibility and viability risk.
The PM leads on value and viability and leads through influence, not command.

Product vocabulary in practice: problem statements, hypotheses and MVPs
Write a problem statement that names a user, a situation and a cost
Turn a feature idea into a testable hypothesis with a measurable signal

Product teams use a small set of words constantly. Using them precisely helps you think clearly and earns trust quickly in a new team. This lesson teaches each term through something you will actually write.
A lightbulb idea becoming a written plan
Problem statements and hypotheses turn a loose idea into something a team can test.
The problem statement

Most bad products start with a solution looking for a problem. A **problem statement** forces you to describe the problem first, without naming a feature. A useful pattern is: **[User] needs a way to [do something] because [situation], which today costs them [time, money, risk].**

Weak: "We need a chat feature." Strong: "Small fashion sellers on Instagram need a way to confirm a customer's payment without leaving their phone, because transfers arrive on a separate banking app, which today causes about 10 minutes of checking per order and sometimes shipping before money has arrived." The strong version tells the team who, when, and why it hurts, and leaves room for many possible solutions.
The hypothesis

A **hypothesis** is a belief you can prove wrong. In product work it links a change to an expected result: **We believe that [change] for [user] will result in [outcome]. We will know we are right when we see [measurable signal] within [time].** If you cannot imagine a result that would prove it wrong, it is an opinion, not a hypothesis.
The MVP

**MVP** means minimum viable product, a term popularised by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup. It is the smallest thing you can put in front of real users to learn whether your hypothesis is true. It is **not** a cheap, broken version of the full product. Sometimes an MVP has no code at all: a WhatsApp number answered by a person, a Google Form, or a manual service delivered behind a simple page.
Worked example: from idea to problem, hypothesis and MVP
For example, Bisi runs product for a small logistics start-up in Ibadan. The founder wants to build a full app so customers can track parcels.
Problem statement: online sellers need to know when a parcel will arrive, because their buyers keep asking, which today means about 15 WhatsApp messages a day per seller to our dispatch office.

Hypothesis: we believe that sending sellers an automatic SMS at pickup and at delivery will cut their "where is my parcel?" messages. We will know we are right when messages to dispatch fall by at least half within four weeks.
MVP: instead of building an app, the dispatch officer sends the two messages manually from a template for 20 sellers for four weeks and counts incoming queries.
Week 4 result: queries from those 20 sellers fall from about 300 a week to about 120 a week, a 60% drop. (300 minus 120 is 180; 180 divided by 300 is 0.6.)
Only now does Bisi ask engineering to automate the messages, a much smaller build than a tracking app.
The team learned that timely notifications, not a full tracking app, solved most of the problem, and they confirmed it in four weeks without writing code.

Each step makes the idea more testable before the team commits serious effort.
Do not change the signal after the test
Write your success signal before the test starts. If the result is disappointing, moving the target afterwards hides the lesson and teaches the team that evidence does not matter.

Finally, notice the difference between **validated learning** and **activity**. Ten meetings, a new logo and a long specification are activity. A test that proved a hypothesis right or wrong is learning. When you report progress, lead with what you learned and what you will do differently. A short weekly note with three lines, what we tested, what we learned, what we will do next, keeps everyone focused on evidence rather than busyness.

Building for African users, and the product career ladder
List practical constraints that shape product decisions for many African users
Apply data protection basics to a product decision in Nigeria

Frameworks from Silicon Valley books travel well, but the users do not always look like the users in those books. A PM building for Nigerian, Ghanaian or Kenyan customers must design for real phones, real networks, real money habits and real laws. Getting these right is often what separates a product that spreads from one that stalls.
A person paying with a mobile phone
Many African products live on a mobile phone, often a low-cost Android device with limited data.
Constraints to design for
**Devices:** many users have entry-level Android phones with little storage. A large app download or heavy images can stop someone installing at all.
**Data cost and coverage:** data is paid for out of pocket and signal drops in many areas. Features should save work locally and retry, rather than lose a form when the network fails.
**Channels beyond apps:** USSD codes, SMS and WhatsApp reach people who will not install an app. Many successful services offer more than one channel.
**Trust and cash:** many customers fear fraud and prefer to see a person. Agent networks, clear receipts and fast human support build trust.
**Language and literacy:** short sentences, icons, local languages and voice notes widen your audience.
**Regulation:** payments, lending and health products need licences or approvals. In Nigeria, payments sit under Central Bank of Nigeria rules, and food or drug products under NAFDAC.
Personal data is a product decision

Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for collecting and processing personal data. Collect only what the feature needs, explain why you need it, protect it, and never put customer phone numbers or account details in screenshots, spreadsheets or WhatsApp groups that are shared widely.
Worked example: adapting a feature for low data
For example, Zainab is PM for an app that lets market traders record daily sales. Interviews show that traders in a busy Kano market often lose their entries when the network drops.
She restates the problem: traders need to record a sale in under 10 seconds even with no signal, because a lost entry means they stop trusting the app.
With the engineers she agrees an offline-first approach: entries save on the phone first, then sync when the network returns, with a small icon showing what has not yet synced.
She reduces the home screen images so the screen loads with less data, and asks the designer to test the flow with three traders using their own phones.
She adds a weekly SMS summary for traders who rarely open the app.
Success signal: the share of traders still recording sales after 30 days rises, measured against the previous month's group.
The feature fits real conditions. The team measures a retention outcome rather than counting how many screens were shipped.

Reachable without the app

Clear in simple language
Licence and data rules checked
Run every major feature through this list before it is approved for delivery.

Product strategy, hiring and coaching PMs

Many PMs did not start as PMs. Customer support staff, business analysts, designers, engineers, teachers and operations officers move across because they already understand users or delivery. Fintech, e-commerce, logistics, health, agriculture and education technology companies across Africa hire PMs, and some international companies hire remotely. Read real job adverts on company career pages and LinkedIn to see what each employer asks for rather than relying on general claims.
Reading a PM job advert

Job adverts mix true requirements with wish lists. Read them in three passes. First, find the **domain**: payments, lending, logistics, health, education. Domain knowledge from your current job is valuable and often decides who gets hired. Second, find the **evidence they ask for**: shipped features, discovery work, metrics you improved, experience working with engineers. Third, find the **tools named**, such as Jira, Figma, SQL or a product analytics tool. Tools can be learned in weeks; evidence of judgement takes longer, so build that first.

Also notice the **channel and market** the role serves. A PM for an agent banking product will spend time with agents in the field and must understand cash handling and fraud. A PM for an international software company may work across time zones with users she never meets in person. Both are product management, but the daily work is very different, so choose deliberately.
Start where you are

If your organisation has a website, app or internal system, offer to collect user feedback, write clear requirements or run a small test. Real evidence from your own workplace makes a stronger case study than an imaginary project.
Design for real devices, unreliable networks, multiple channels, trust and local language.
Data protection and licensing are product decisions, not afterthoughts.
Product levels differ mainly in the size of decisions you are trusted with.

Discovery, Prioritisation and Delivery

The core working cycle of a product manager: find and test the riskiest assumptions, choose what to build with a structured and explainable method, and write work so a development team builds the right thing. Each lesson produces a document you will reuse in the capstone.
Discovery: assumption mapping and interviews that reveal real behaviour
List the assumptions hidden inside a product idea
Rank assumptions by importance and evidence on an assumption map
Ask interview questions about past behaviour instead of opinions
Set up a simple discovery workspace with free tools

Every product idea is a bundle of beliefs. "Pharmacies will reorder stock through our app" quietly assumes that pharmacists have smartphones, trust a new supplier, can pay digitally, and reorder often enough to bother. Discovery starts by making those beliefs visible, then testing the most dangerous ones first.
Two people in conversation across a table
A good discovery interview listens to what people actually did, not what they say they might do.
Step 1: write the assumptions

Take the idea and write every belief that must be true for it to succeed. Group them under the four risks from Module 1: value (they want it), usability (they can use it), feasibility (we can build it) and viability (it works for the business). Aim for at least 10. Write each as a statement that could be false, for example "Pharmacists reorder at least once a week".
Step 2: map them

**Assumption mapping**, described by David J. Bland in Testing Business Ideas, places each assumption on two axes: how **important** it is to success, and how much **evidence** you already have. The top-left quadrant, important but with little evidence, holds your riskiest assumptions. Test those first.
Assumption map
Test first: critical, no evidence
Monitor: critical, proven
Park for now
Safe to ignore
Evidence: weak to strong
Importance: low to high
Sort each assumption into a quadrant and start testing in the top-left.
Step 3: interview about the past

People are kind. If you describe your idea and ask "Would you use this?", most will say yes. Rob Fitzpatrick's book The Mom Test gives three rules to avoid this trap: talk about **their life, not your idea**; ask about **specific past events, not hypothetical futures**; and **talk less, listen more**. Past behaviour is the best evidence you can get in a conversation.
Weak question
Better question
Would you use an app to reorder stock?
Tell me about the last time you ran out of a product. What happened?
How much would you pay for this?
What do you spend now to solve this? Who do you pay?
Do you think this is a good idea?
What have you already tried? Why did you stop?
Would you recommend it?
When did you last tell someone about a supplier? What did you say?
Recruit 5 to 8 people who match the target user. Ask permission to take notes and explain how you will store them.
Open with context: their work, their week, the task you care about.
Ask for the last specific time the problem happened. Follow up with "What did you do next?" and "What did that cost you?"
Do not pitch. If they ask about your idea, say you will share it at the end.
Within an hour, write facts, quotes and surprises separately from your own interpretation.
Worked example: one week of discovery
For example, Halima is exploring a stock reordering app for small pharmacies in Abuja. Her team listed 14 assumptions.
On the map, two land in the top-left: "pharmacists reorder at least weekly" and "pharmacists will pay a new supplier before delivery".
She interviews 6 pharmacists about their last reorder. 5 of 6 reorder at least weekly, usually by phone call or WhatsApp to a known sales representative. The first assumption gains evidence.
On payment, 5 of 6 describe paying on delivery or on credit with suppliers they have known for years. Only 1 has ever paid before delivery to a new supplier.
She moves the payment assumption to "critical, evidence against" and writes a new question: could the product work with pay-on-delivery through a trusted logistics partner?
She records the evidence in a shared sheet with columns: assumption, quadrant, test, result, date, next step.
In one week, with no code, Halima found that the original payment model would likely fail and redirected the team before engineering work began.
Other quick tests

Interviews are not the only way to gather evidence. A **fake door test** shows a button or menu item for a feature that does not exist yet and counts how many people tap it, followed by an honest message that it is coming soon. A **concierge test** delivers the service by hand to a few customers. A **prototype test** asks five users to complete a task on a clickable design. Choose the cheapest test that would actually change your decision.

**Google Sheets or Excel:** assumption log, interview tracker, scoring tables.
**Google Docs or Notion:** interview notes and one-page summaries.
**Miro or FigJam:** online whiteboards for assumption maps and story maps.
**Google Forms:** short follow-up surveys after interviews, never instead of them.
**Figma (view or comment access):** review designs and prototypes with your designer.
**Trello, Jira or Linear:** where the team's backlog lives once work is chosen.
Protect interview data
Store notes with first names or codes only, keep recordings in an access-controlled folder, delete them when the project ends, and never share personal details in public channels.

Prioritising with an opportunity solution tree, Kano and weighted scoring
Build an opportunity solution tree from one outcome
Classify features with the Kano model

After discovery you will have more good ideas than time. Prioritisation is choosing what to do **now** and being able to explain why. A ranked list without reasoning invites endless argument. A ranked list with visible reasoning lets people disagree with the inputs instead of with you.
A person arranging items in order of importance
Prioritisation is deciding the order, and showing the reasoning behind it.
How this differs from growth scoring

If you have taken Growth Marketing, you met ICE and RICE for ranking experiments. Here we focus on deciding which customer problems and product features to invest in, using tools that keep the customer need visible.
Start with the opportunity solution tree

Teresa Torres, author of Continuous Discovery Habits, describes the **opportunity solution tree**. At the top is one **outcome** the team is asked to move. Below it are **opportunities**: customer needs, pain points and desires found in discovery. Below each opportunity are **solutions** that might address it, and below those are **assumption tests**. The tree stops teams jumping straight from a goal to a favourite feature, and makes it obvious when five solutions all target one minor need.
Opportunity solution tree
Outcome
Opportunities (customer needs)
Solutions
Assumption tests
Work from the top down: choose an opportunity before comparing solutions.
Kano: not all features satisfy in the same way

The **Kano model**, developed by Professor Noriaki Kano, sorts features by how they affect satisfaction. **Must-be** features cause anger when missing but little delight when present, such as a receipt after payment. **Performance** features raise satisfaction the better they are, such as transfer speed. **Attractive** features delight when present but are not expected, such as a friendly birthday message. **Indifferent** features do not matter to users at all. A product needs its must-be features before attractive ones make any difference.
MoSCoW: agree the scope of a release

**MoSCoW** labels items for a fixed release: **Must have** (the release fails without it), **Should have** (important but there is a workaround), **Could have** (nice if time allows), and **Won't have this time** (agreed out of scope). It was created by Dai Clegg and is widely used in the DSDM agile method. Its value is the honest "Won't" list, which prevents silent scope creep.
Weighted scoring: make trade-offs visible

Pick three to five criteria that match your outcome, give each a weight that adds to 100%, score each option from 1 to 5, multiply and add. Agree the criteria and weights **before** scoring so nobody tunes the numbers to favour a pet idea.
Worked example: ranking three options for a pharmacy app

For example, Halima's outcome is "more pharmacies placing a second order within 30 days". Discovery found three opportunities, each with one candidate solution. The team agrees criteria: customer impact 40%, strategic fit 25%, confidence from evidence 20%, ease of build 15% (5 means easiest).
Option A, pay-on-delivery via logistics partner: impact 5, fit 4, confidence 4, ease 2. Score = 5x0.40 + 4x0.25 + 4x0.20 + 2x0.15 = 2.00 + 1.00 + 0.80 + 0.30 = 4.10.
Option B, one-tap reorder of last basket: impact 4, fit 5, confidence 3, ease 4. Score = 1.60 + 1.25 + 0.60 + 0.60 = 4.05.
Option C, loyalty points: impact 2, fit 3, confidence 2, ease 3. Score = 0.80 + 0.75 + 0.40 + 0.45 = 2.40.
A and B are almost tied, so Halima checks Kano: interviews showed paying on delivery is a must-be for most pharmacists, while one-tap reorder is a performance feature.
MoSCoW for the next release: Must, pay-on-delivery; Should, one-tap reorder; Won't this time, loyalty points.
The team builds A first, plans B next, and drops C for now. Anyone can read the table and see which inputs to challenge if they disagree.

Choosing good criteria and weights

Criteria should come from the outcome and the company strategy, not from habit. If the outcome is retention, "customer impact" should mean impact on returning customers, not on sign-ups. Keep to five criteria at most; more criteria make the table look scientific while hiding the real trade-off. Include **confidence** as a criterion so an exciting idea with no evidence cannot easily beat a modest idea that interviews strongly support.

Score as a group: the PM proposes scores, engineers own the ease scores, and the designer and support lead challenge the impact scores. Write one line of justification next to each score, for example "5 of 6 pharmacists described this problem unprompted". When the scores are done, step back and ask whether the result makes sense. If it does not, the table has revealed a missing criterion or a wrong assumption, which is useful too.
When the loudest voice disagrees
Invite the stakeholder to change a score or a weight in the open, with evidence. If the ranking changes, the decision is better. If not, they can see why.

Write acceptance criteria in Given, When, Then form
Slice a large feature into small, valuable stories using a story map

Once a feature is chosen, the team needs to know exactly what "done" means. Vague requests such as "add pay on delivery" lead to rework, arguments and features that work in a demo but fail in the market. This lesson gives you the formats most agile teams use to prevent that.
A team board with task cards in columns
Well-written stories move cleanly across the team's board from to-do to done.
The user story

The common template, first used at the company Connextra, is: **As a [type of user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].** The benefit is the most important part: it tells engineers and designers why the story exists, so they can suggest a simpler way to achieve it. A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a full specification.
Weak: "As a user, I want a button." Strong: "As a pharmacist placing an order, I want to choose pay on delivery, so that I only pay once the stock is in my hands."
Check it with INVEST

Bill Wake proposed INVEST as a checklist for good stories. **Independent:** can be built without waiting for another story. **Negotiable:** details can be discussed. **Valuable:** delivers something a user or the business cares about. **Estimable:** the team can size it. **Small:** fits comfortably in one sprint or iteration. **Testable:** you can prove it works.
Acceptance criteria

Acceptance criteria are the conditions a story must meet to be accepted. The **Given, When, Then** format from behaviour-driven development makes them precise: **Given** a starting situation, **When** the user does something, **Then** a specific result happens. Cover the normal path and the important failure paths.
Worked example: stories and criteria for pay on delivery
For example, Halima now writes the Must-have feature from the last lesson for her team's next two-week sprint.
Story: As a pharmacist placing an order, I want to choose pay on delivery, so that I only pay once the stock is in my hands.

Criterion 1: Given a verified pharmacy with an order under the agreed limit, when the pharmacist selects pay on delivery, then the order is confirmed and the summary shows "Pay the rider on delivery" with the total.
Criterion 2: Given an order above the limit, when the pharmacist selects pay on delivery, then the app explains the limit and offers to split the order or pay now.
Criterion 3: Given a confirmed pay-on-delivery order, when the rider records payment, then the pharmacist receives an SMS receipt within one minute.
INVEST check: the team estimates it fits in the sprint, it is testable through the three criteria, and it does not depend on the reorder feature.
Engineers, the designer and the tester share one clear definition of done, including what happens when an order is too large.
Story mapping and slicing

Jeff Patton's **user story mapping** lays the user's journey left to right as big steps (the backbone), with detailed stories stacked under each step. You then draw horizontal lines to slice releases. The first slice is the thinnest path that lets a user complete the whole journey, even if each step is basic.
Story map backbone for ordering stock
Find product
Build order
Choose payment
Track delivery
Receive and confirm
Release 1 takes the simplest story under each step, so the full journey works end to end.
**Slice by path:** the happy path first, rare error cases later (unless they risk money or safety).
**Slice by data:** one product category or one city first.
**Slice by rule:** a fixed order limit first, personalised limits later.
**Slice by interface:** a simple list first, search and filters later.
Definition of done and working with the team

Acceptance criteria are specific to one story. The **definition of done** is the team's shared quality standard for every story, for example: code reviewed, tested on a low-end Android phone, tracking events added, support guide updated. In Scrum, the Scrum Guide describes the product owner as accountable for the product backlog, including ordering it and making items clear. A story is only finished when it meets both its criteria and the definition of done.

Write stories with the team, not for them. Bring a draft to a short refinement session, let engineers ask questions and propose simpler options, and update the story there and then. During the sprint, stay available: a question answered in ten minutes saves a day of building the wrong thing. After review, if something was misunderstood, improve how you write the next story instead of blaming the team.
Do not slice away the safety
Never postpone criteria that protect money or personal data, such as payment confirmation, limits, receipts and access control, to make a story smaller. Slice features, not safeguards.
A user story names a real user, a capability and a benefit.
INVEST is a quick quality check before a story enters a sprint.
Given, When, Then criteria define done, including failure paths.
Story maps help you release the thinnest complete journey first; never slice away safeguards.

Stakeholders, Roadmaps, Consulting and Your Portfolio

Product work succeeds or fails in conversations with stakeholders, so this module covers discovery with clients and leaders, honest roadmaps, scoping paid product work, and measuring results after launch. You finish with a case-study outline and a 90-day plan.
Stakeholder discovery and an honest Now-Next-Later roadmap
Run a stakeholder discovery conversation with a structured question set
Map stakeholders by influence and interest and plan how to engage each group
Build a Now-Next-Later roadmap organised around problems and outcomes
Communicate a change of priority without losing trust

Whether you join a company as a PM or advise one as a consultant, your first weeks are discovery of a different kind: understanding the business, the people and the politics. A roadmap built without that understanding will be ignored or overturned.
A small team meeting around a table
Stakeholder conversations reveal goals, constraints and disagreements before you plan.
Questions for your first conversations
Area
Questions to ask
Stage and goals
Is the product still finding fit, growing, or being optimised? What one result would make this year a success?
Evidence
What do we already know about users, from research, analytics or support? Where are the biggest gaps?
Capacity
How many engineers and designers do we have? What is already committed?
Constraints
Which regulations, partner contracts or technical limits must we respect?
Alignment
Where do leaders disagree about direction? What decision has been stuck for months?
Decision rights
Who decides priorities, and who must be consulted or simply informed?

Listen more than you speak in these conversations, and write down the exact words people use for problems. When two leaders describe the goal differently, do not choose between them in the meeting. Note the difference and bring it to the person with decision rights, with the evidence, so the disagreement is settled once rather than fought feature by feature.
Map the people

List everyone who affects or is affected by the product, then place them by **influence** (power over decisions) and **interest** (how much they care). People with high influence and high interest, such as the founder or head of operations, need close collaboration. High influence, low interest people, such as the finance director, need to be kept satisfied with short, relevant updates. Low influence, high interest people, such as support agents, should be kept informed and are often your best source of customer signals.
Stakeholder map
Keep satisfied
Manage closely
Monitor
Keep informed
Interest: low to high
Influence: low to high
Decide how often and how deeply to engage each group before conflicts appear.
The Now-Next-Later roadmap

Janna Bastow, co-founder of ProdPad, created the **Now-Next-Later** roadmap after seeing timeline roadmaps fail. It drops dates and uses three columns. **Now:** problems the team is actively working on, well understood. **Next:** problems being explored and likely to come soon. **Later:** important problems that are still uncertain. Each item is written as a problem or outcome, not a feature, so the team keeps room to find the best solution. Uncertainty grows from left to right, which is honest.
Worked example: turning a feature list into a roadmap
For example, Ifeoma joins a Port Harcourt school-payments start-up as its first PM. The founder hands her a list of 18 requested features with promised dates.
She holds six stakeholder conversations using the question table and learns the company goal is to cut late school-fee payments for its 40 partner schools.
She groups the 18 features under four problems: parents forget due dates, parents cannot pay in instalments, schools cannot see who has paid, and receipts are lost.
Now: "Parents forget due dates" (SMS and WhatsApp reminders, already validated with two schools).
Next: "Schools cannot see who has paid" (dashboard, discovery under way). Later: "Instalment payments" (needs a licensed partner and a viability check).
She shares the roadmap with a note: items in Now have target months; Next and Later do not, and will be reviewed on the first Monday of every month.
The founder can see every request accounted for, linked to a problem and a company goal, without the team being trapped by dates nobody could promise.
Changing priorities without losing trust

When evidence changes a priority, tell the affected stakeholders before the roadmap changes, in person or by a short call. Say what you learned, what changes, what does not, and when you will review again. Surprises damage trust more than bad news.
Presenting the roadmap

Different audiences need different versions of the same roadmap. Leadership wants to see how each column links to company goals and what the team is deliberately not doing. Engineers want to know what is coming next so they can prepare technically. Sales and support want to know what they can tell customers, so give them clear wording: "we are working on this now" is safe to say; items in Later are not promises and should not be shared with customers as if they were.

Keep the roadmap to one page and review it on a fixed rhythm, such as monthly. In the review, move items only when evidence or company goals have changed, and record why. A roadmap that changes every week because of whoever spoke last is a sign that prioritisation, not the roadmap, needs fixing.

Finally, keep a short **decision log**: date, decision, options considered, evidence, who decided. When someone asks six months later why the team chose A over B, the log answers it in a minute and protects the team from repeating old arguments.
Start with stakeholder discovery: goals, evidence, capacity, constraints, alignment and decision rights.

Explain priority changes early and keep a decision log.

Fractional product work: proposals, pricing logic and scope control
Describe common types of freelance and fractional product engagements
Calculate a day rate from your own income target and working days
Write a scope of work with deliverables, exclusions and a change process
Handle a scope change request professionally

Most PMs are employed, but early-stage companies, NGOs and small businesses often need product skills before they can afford a full-time hire. **Fractional** product management means working a fixed share of the week for a client, for example two days a week for three months. Other engagements are fixed projects, such as a four-week discovery sprint or a roadmap workshop.
A signed agreement document
A written scope protects both you and the client from misunderstandings.
Common engagement types
Engagement
Typical deliverables
Pricing basis
Discovery sprint
Interview summary, assumption map, recommended opportunity
Fixed project fee
Roadmap and prioritisation
Stakeholder interviews, opportunity tree, Now-Next-Later roadmap
Fractional PM
Ongoing backlog, stories, sprint support, monthly report
Monthly retainer for agreed days
Backlog clean-up
Rewritten stories with acceptance criteria for top items
Fixed fee or day rate
Working out your price

There is no official rate card for product consulting in Nigeria, and rates vary widely with experience, client size and whether the client pays in naira or foreign currency. Rather than copying a number from social media, calculate your own floor from your needs, then adjust after checking what comparable consultants and clients in your network actually pay.
Worked example: from income target to a project quote
For example, Ngozi has three years as a business analyst and wants to offer fractional product work. All figures here are illustrative, not market rates.
She sets a monthly income target of 1,200,000 naira before tax and business costs.
She adds business costs (data, laptop replacement savings, software, pension) of about 200,000 naira, so she needs 1,400,000 naira a month.
Of about 20 working days a month, she expects 14 to be billable; the rest go to sales, admin and learning. Day rate floor = 1,400,000 / 14 = 100,000 naira.
A discovery sprint needs about 8 days: 2 planning and stakeholder interviews, 3 user interviews and notes, 2 synthesis and mapping, 1 presentation. 8 x 100,000 = 800,000 naira.
She adds 15% contingency for coordination: 800,000 x 0.15 = 120,000, giving a quote of 920,000 naira, with 40% due at signing and 60% on delivery.
Ngozi's quote is grounded in real days of work and her own costs, so she can explain it calmly and knows the lowest price she can accept.
What a scope of work must say
**Objective:** the outcome the client wants, in one sentence.
**Deliverables:** each document or session, with format and number, for example "one 60-minute roadmap workshop and a written roadmap".
**Client responsibilities:** access to people, data and decisions by agreed dates.
**Exclusions:** what is not included, such as design work, writing code or managing the development team after handover.
**Timeline and reviews:** dates for drafts, feedback windows and final delivery.
**Fees and payment terms:** amount, schedule, method and what happens if payment is late.
**Change process:** how new requests are priced and approved before any extra work starts.
Handling a change request
Client asks for extra
Check against scope
Estimate days and impact
Offer options in writing
Proceed after written approval
Every addition goes through the same path, so scope never grows silently.

When a client asks for something new, do not say yes in the meeting. Thank them, check the scope, then offer clear options in writing: add it for an extra fee and time, swap it for something of similar size, or move it to a later phase. Keep a running change log that both sides can see.
Writing the proposal

Before the scope of work, send a short proposal of one or two pages. Open with the client's problem in their own words from your first conversation, then the outcome you will help them reach, your approach in three to five steps, what they will receive, the timeline, and the fee. Offer two options where possible, for example a smaller discovery-only package and a fuller package that adds a roadmap workshop. Options let the client choose scope without negotiating your rate down.

End with a clear next step, such as "reply to confirm and I will send the agreement and first invoice". After each engagement, ask for a short written testimonial and permission to describe the work, with confidential details removed, in your portfolio. Over time, real outcomes from past clients are what justify higher rates. Review your day rate at least once a year against your costs and the demand you are seeing.
Payment and contract safety

Ask for a deposit before work starts, invoice from a business account in your registered name, confirm payments in your own banking app rather than trusting screenshots, and never share client data you received during discovery with anyone outside the engagement. For larger contracts, ask a lawyer to review the agreement.
Fractional and project-based product work suits clients not ready for a full-time PM.

Launch, measure, learn: your product case study and 90-day plan
Choose outcome and guardrail measures for a release using the HEART framework
Run a short launch checklist and a post-launch review
Structure a product case study that shows reasoning, not just results
Write a focused 90-day plan toward a product role or engagement

Shipping is the middle of the work, not the end. A PM decides before launch what to measure, watches what actually happens, and turns the result into the next decision. Those habits also produce the evidence that makes a strong portfolio.
A rocket launching from a laptop screen
Launch day is when the measuring starts, not when the work stops.
Decide what to measure: HEART

Google researchers led by Kerry Rodden published the **HEART** framework for user-centred metrics: **Happiness** (satisfaction, often from short surveys), **Engagement** (how often or deeply people use the feature), **Adoption** (new users of the feature), **Retention** (people who keep coming back), and **Task success** (completion rate, time, errors). Pick the one or two that match your outcome, then for each define a **goal**, a **signal** you can observe, and a **metric** you can calculate.
Add a **guardrail**: a measure that must not get worse, such as payment errors, complaints or support calls. A feature that raises orders but doubles failed deliveries is not a success.
A simple launch checklist
Acceptance criteria tested, including failure paths and money handling.
Tracking events working, so you can calculate the chosen metrics from day one.
Support team briefed with a short guide and answers to likely questions.
Release plan agreed: a small group or one city first, then wider.
Rollback plan: how to switch the feature off if the guardrail is breached.
Worked example: reading launch results
For example, Halima's team releases pay on delivery to 1,200 active pharmacies. Before launch, 38% of new pharmacies placed a second order within 30 days.
Adoption: in the first 30 days, 300 pharmacies use pay on delivery. 300 / 1,200 = 25% adoption.
Retention outcome: for pharmacies joining after launch, 46% place a second order within 30 days, up 8 percentage points from 38%.
Guardrail: failed deliveries rise from 3% to 5% of orders, mostly orders above the limit where riders carry large sums.
Decision: keep the feature, lower the order limit and add a rider safety rule, then review in 30 days.
She notes the caveat: other changes happened that month, so she will compare with the next cohort before claiming the full 8 points.
The team learned the feature worked, found a safety cost, acted on it, and reported honestly about what the numbers can and cannot prove.
The post-launch learning loop
Set goal and guardrail
Release to a small group
Measure signals
Review and decide
Update roadmap
Every release feeds the next decision, which is how product judgement improves.
The post-launch review

About 30 days after release, hold a one-hour review with the team. Compare the metrics with the goals you wrote before launch, look at the guardrails, read a sample of support messages and user feedback, and agree one of three decisions: **keep and improve**, **change direction**, or **remove the feature**. Removing a feature that does not work is a sign of discipline, not failure, because every feature adds maintenance and support cost.

Write the review as a short note: what we expected, what happened, what we think caused it, what we will do next. File it with your decision log. These notes are the raw material for your case study and, over time, for better instincts about which ideas are likely to work.
Your product case study

Hiring managers want to see how you think. A strong case study is two to four pages or a short slide set, with confidential details removed and permission obtained for any real company work. Use this structure:
**Context:** the product, users and the outcome you were asked to move.
**Discovery:** your assumptions, how you tested them, and what surprised you.
**Prioritisation:** the options, the framework and the reasoning for the choice.
**Delivery:** two or three example stories with acceptance criteria.
**Results and reflection:** what happened, or for a practice project what you would measure, and what you would do differently.

Keep it readable on a phone: short headings, one diagram or table per section, and your key decision visible on the first page. Link to supporting files, such as the scoring sheet or story map, rather than pasting everything in.
Honesty is a strength
If a decision did not work, say so and show what you learned. Reflection on a disappointing result demonstrates more product judgement than a list of successes with no reasoning.
Your 90-day plan

Name one target: for example, an associate PM role at a fintech or agritech company, a product role inside your current employer, or two fractional clients. Then plan three 30-day blocks: **days 1 to 30**, finish your capstone case study and update your LinkedIn profile with it; **days 31 to 60**, do one real discovery project for a local business or NGO and talk to three working PMs; **days 61 to 90**, apply to specific roles or pitch specific clients, tracking each application and the feedback you get.
Use HEART to choose a goal, signal and metric, and always add a guardrail.
Launch to a small group first with tracking, briefed support and a rollback plan.
Report results honestly, including caveats and safety costs.

A product team can write excellent code and still fail. The app works, but people do not use it, or the business still loses money.
The product manager, or PM, is the person whose job is to reduce that danger. She does not usually write the code or draw the screens.
She decides, with the team, what problem to solve next, for whom, and how we will know it worked.
By the end of this module you will frame a product problem as an outcome, a set of risks and a hypothesis you can test.
The first habit
Output
A new screen
A feature
A release
Ticked off on release day
More traders paying suppliers
Fewer failed deliveries
Fewer calls to support
You wait and watch behaviour
An output is something the team ships: a new screen, a feature, a release. Outputs are easy to count, so weak teams celebrate them.

An outcome is a change in what people do that matters to the business. Here is a simple test. If you can tick it off on release day, it is an output. If you must wait and watch user behaviour, it is an outcome.
A feature nobody uses is cost without value.
Every idea carries them
The four big product risks
Value: will they use it? (PM)
Usability: can they use it? (designer)
Feasibility: can we build it? (engineer)
Viability: does it work for us? (PM)
Every idea carries four risks. Value: will customers choose to use it? The PM leads here.
Usability: can users figure it out? The designer leads.
Feasibility: can our engineers build it with the time and skills we have?
Viability: does it work for legal, finance, support and partners? The PM owns this too. An idea is ready only with evidence on all four.
Worked example
Amaka checks a savings idea
6 of the last 40 support chats asked about fixed savings. A signal, not proof.
The ledger can hold end dates. A first version is about two weeks of work.
Finance must confirm the higher rate. Compliance must check the licence.
Here is a worked example. Amaka is PM for a savings app used by market traders in Lagos. A director wants traders to lock savings for 90 days for a higher rate.
On value, 6 of the last 40 support chats asked about fixed savings. That is a signal, not proof.
On feasibility, the engineer says a first version is about two weeks of work.
But viability is open, so Amaka parks the idea until finance and compliance answer. That saves the team from building something that might be withdrawn.
Step by step
Write your success signal before the test starts.
Problem: user, situation, cost. No feature.
Hypothesis: change, result, signal, time
MVP: the smallest test, maybe no code
Measure the signal honestly
Step one. Write a problem statement: the user, the situation and what it costs them today, without naming a feature.
Step two. Write a hypothesis, a belief you can prove wrong, with a measurable signal and a time limit.
Step three. Design an MVP, a minimum viable product. It is the smallest test that teaches you something, not a broken cheap product. It may be just a WhatsApp number or a Google Form.
Then measure, and build, change or drop the idea.
The common mistake is moving the target after a disappointing result. That hides the lesson. Write your signal first.
Bisi tests before building an app
Before the test
Founder wants a full tracking app
About 300 queries a week
From 20 sellers
After 4 weeks
Manual SMS at pickup and delivery
About 120 queries a week
A 60% drop, no code

Bisi runs product for a logistics start-up in Ibadan. The founder wants a full tracking app. Bisi tests a cheaper idea first: an SMS at pickup and at delivery, sent by hand to 20 sellers for four weeks.
Queries fall from about 300 a week to about 120. That is a 60% drop with no code written. Only now does she ask engineering to automate the messages.
Build for real users
Many users have entry-level phones, costly data and patchy signal. Run every major feature through this check.
Does it work on entry-level Android and survive a dropped network? Can people reach it by USSD, SMS or WhatsApp? Does it build trust, in simple language?
And check the licence and data rules. Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, collect only what you need.
Key points
Remember
Measure outcomes, not just outputs
Check value, usability, feasibility, viability
Problem first, without naming a feature
Signal and time limit written before the test
An MVP is the smallest test, not a broken product

To remember. Measure outcomes, not just outputs. Check every idea for all four risks. Start with the problem, not a feature. Write your signal and time limit before you test. And keep your MVP as small as possible.

Your practice tasks

Score an app on the context checklist
Compare two real PM job adverts

Discover, prioritise and write stories your team can build
Discover, prioritise, and write stories your team can build.
This is the video for module two of Product Management Foundations.
The core cycle
Three jobs in one working cycle
Find and test the riskiest assumptions
Choose what to build, and explain why
Write work so the team builds it right
Every product idea is a bundle of beliefs. Discovery makes those beliefs visible and tests the most dangerous ones first.
Then you will have more good ideas than time, so you must choose what to do now, with reasoning people can see.
Finally, you write the chosen work so clearly that the team builds the right thing, including what happens when things go wrong.
Map assumptions, then test the riskiest
Test first: critical, with little evidence.
Write at least 10 beliefs that could be false
Rate each: how important, how much evidence
Pick the important ones with weak evidence
Test them in the cheapest useful way
Step one. Write every belief that must be true, at least 10, grouped under value, usability, feasibility and viability. For example, pharmacists reorder at least once a week.
Step two. Place each one on an assumption map: how important is it, and how much evidence do you already have?

Step three. Test the ones that are critical but have little evidence. Use an interview, a fake door test, a concierge test or a prototype, whichever is cheapest and would actually change your decision.
This is the rule. Critical and unproven goes first.
Interviews
Ask about the past, not your idea
Would you use an app for this?
How much would you pay?
Is this a good idea?
Tell me about the last time...
What do you spend now?
What have you already tried?
People are kind. If you ask, would you use this, most will say yes. That tells you nothing. This is the most common discovery mistake.
Instead, ask about specific past events. Tell me about the last time you ran out of stock. What did you do next? What did it cost you? Talk less and listen more, and do not pitch.
Worked example
Halima's week of discovery
Two land in the riskiest corner: weekly reordering, and paying a new supplier before delivery.
5 of 6 pharmacists reorder at least weekly, by phone call or WhatsApp.
Only 1 of 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. The payment model must change.
For example, Halima is exploring a stock reordering app for small pharmacies in Abuja. Her team lists 14 assumptions, and two land in the riskiest corner.
She interviews 6 pharmacists about their last reorder. 5 of 6 reorder at least weekly. That assumption gains evidence.
But only 1 of the 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. In one week, with no code, Halima finds the payment model would likely fail, and redirects the team to pay on delivery.
Prioritising
Weighted scoring, step by step
Agree criteria and weights before anyone scores.
Pick 3 to 5 criteria from your outcome
Give weights that add to 100%
Score each option from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and treat small gaps as ties
Halima's outcome is more pharmacies placing a second order within 30 days. Her team agrees four criteria: customer impact 40%, strategic fit 25%, confidence from evidence 20%, and ease of build 15%.
They score each option from 1 to 5. Engineers own the ease scores.

Pay on delivery scores 4.10. One-tap reorder scores 4.05. Loyalty points score 2.40. A gap of 0.05 is a tie, so Halima checks what users expect: paying on delivery is a must-have for most pharmacists.
Agree the criteria first, so nobody tunes the numbers to favour a pet idea. Then label the release: Must, pay on delivery. Should, one-tap reorder. Won't this time, loyalty points.
Write a story the team can build
As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Given, When, Then criteria
Cover the failure paths too
Now write the work. As a pharmacist placing an order, I want to choose pay on delivery, so that I only pay once the stock is in my hands. The benefit tells the team why it matters.
Check it with INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable.
Then write acceptance criteria. Given an order above the limit, when the pharmacist selects pay on delivery, then the app explains the limit and offers to split the order or pay now.
Cover the normal path and the important failure paths. A third criterion promises an SMS receipt within one minute of payment.
Protect money and data
Slice features, never safeguards
Payment confirmation
Limits
Receipts
Access control
When you slice a big feature into small stories, release the thinnest journey that works end to end.
But never cut the criteria that protect money or personal data to make a story smaller.
Payment confirmation, limits, receipts and access control stay in. Slice features, not safeguards.
Key points
Remember
Test important, unproven assumptions first
Ask about past behaviour, not opinions
Agree criteria before scoring
Stories name user, capability and benefit
Criteria cover failure paths; keep safeguards

To remember. Test the important, unproven assumptions first. Ask about past behaviour, not opinions. Agree criteria before scoring. Write stories with a real user and a benefit. And write criteria that cover failure, without slicing away safeguards.
Practice tasks
Your practice tasks
Write three delivery-ready stories

Roadmaps, pricing your product work, and measuring launches
Roadmaps, pricing your product work, and measuring launches.
This is the video for module three of Product Management Foundations.
Why this matters
Product work lives in conversations
Understand the people and the politics
Build an honest roadmap
Price and scope paid work
Measure what happens after launch
Product work succeeds or fails in conversations with stakeholders. A roadmap built without understanding the business, the people and the politics will be ignored or overturned.
In this module you learn to build an honest roadmap, price and scope paid product work, and measure results after launch. You finish with a case study outline and a 90-day plan.
Roadmaps
Feature list versus Now-Next-Later
Feature list
18 features with promised dates
Dates nobody can keep
Team trapped by promises
Now-Next-Later
Now: parents forget due dates
Next: who has paid?
Later: instalment payments
For example, Ifeoma joins a school-payments start-up in Port Harcourt as its first PM. The founder hands her 18 requested features with promised dates.

After six stakeholder conversations, she groups the features under problems. Now holds the problem that is understood: parents forget due dates. Next holds what is being explored. Later holds instalments, which need a licensed partner.
Each item is a problem, not a feature, and only Now gets target months. That is honest about uncertainty.
Keep trust
When a priority changes
Surprises damage trust more than bad news.
Tell affected people before the roadmap changes
Say what you learned
Say what changes and what does not
Say when you will review again
Record it in your decision log
When evidence changes a priority, tell the affected stakeholders first, in person or by a short call. Say what you learned, and what changes and what does not.
Say when you will review again, and write the decision in a short log: date, options, evidence, and who decided.
Remember, surprises damage trust more than bad news.
Worked example
Ngozi prices a discovery sprint
For example, Ngozi, a business analyst for three years, wants to offer fractional product work.
Monthly need, with costs
Day rate floor (14 billable days)
Sprint of 8 days
15% contingency
Illustrative figures, not market rates.

Fractional means working a fixed share of the week for a client. There is no official rate card, so do not copy a number from social media. Calculate your own floor. These figures are illustrative, not market rates.
Ngozi needs 1,400,000 naira a month, including business costs. Of about 20 working days, she expects only 14 to be billable. 1,400,000 divided by 14 gives a day rate floor of 100,000 naira.
A discovery sprint takes about 8 days, so 800,000 naira. She adds 15% for coordination, which is 120,000.
Her quote is 920,000 naira, with 40% at signing and 60% on delivery. Because it is built from real days and real costs, she can explain it calmly.
Protect your money
Scope and payment safeguards
Deliverables and exclusions in writing
A change process before extra work
Deposit before work starts
Confirm payments in your bank app
Never share client data
Write a scope of work with deliverables, exclusions and a change process. When a client asks for something new, never say yes in the meeting. Offer written options first.
Ask for a deposit before you start, and confirm payments in your own banking app, not from screenshots. Never share client data from discovery.
Reading launch results honestly
300 of 1,200 active pharmacies used pay on delivery in the first 30 days.
Second orders within 30 days rose from 38% to 46% for new pharmacies.
Failed deliveries rose, mostly large orders. Lower the limit, add a rider safety rule.
Before launch, decide what to measure, and add a guardrail, a number that must not get worse. Halima releases pay on delivery to 1,200 pharmacies. In 30 days, 300 use it. That is 25% adoption.
Pharmacies placing a second order within 30 days rise from 38% to 46%.

But failed deliveries rise from 3% to 5%, mostly large orders where riders carry big sums. So she keeps the feature, lowers the order limit, adds a rider safety rule, and reports honestly that other changes that month may explain part of the gain.
Your portfolio
A case study that shows your thinking
Context: users and the outcome
Discovery: assumptions and tests
Prioritisation: options and reasons
Delivery: stories with criteria
Results and reflection
Hiring managers want to see how you think. Write two to four pages: the context, your discovery, and how you chose between options.
Add two or three stories with criteria, then results and reflection. If a decision did not work, say so and show what you learned.
Key points
Remember
Roadmap problems, not features
Explain priority changes early
Price from your costs and billable days
Written options for every scope change
Measure with a guardrail; report honestly

To remember. Put problems on your roadmap, not features. Explain priority changes early. Price from your own costs and billable days. Handle every scope change in writing. And measure with a guardrail, then report honestly.

Your practice tasks
Write a measurement plan
Write your 90-day plan
